title: TODO.md — punch list
text:
Always check TODO.md before starting work. Update it as tasks land ([x]), start ([~]), or get skipped ([-]). See LOG.md for the history behind any line, METHODOLOGY.md for the data/scope rules, and PLAN.md for the full phased build order.



Remove the nested rva-sourcebook/ duplicate subfolder (superseded by root files).
Remove stale generic scaffold: rva-sourcebook.qmd, app.R, _site/.
Rewrite PLAN.md — was a Fauquier County/Better Housing Coalition plan for an unrelated engagement.
Rewrite CLAUDE.md — fix geography section (rr/bhc/secondary/ashland/regions, not pha/4-primary), switch book → website language, drop PHA/BHC client-review conventions, add mapgl section, trim “Known gotchas” to what’s real.
Reset this file to a real, accurate punch list.
Write README.md (quick start, renv guide, status).
Write METHODOLOGY.md (geography/scope conventions, referenced by CLAUDE.md but never written).
Reconcile _quarto.yml — real navbar (Home/About/Inventory/Demographics/Market/Data Notes), output-dir: docs, freeze: auto, execute-dir: project. Added stub content to inventory.qmd/demographics.qmd/market.qmd/data-notes.qmd/index.qmd/about.qmd so the site renders end-to-end even before real data lands.
First LOG.md entry for this session.
Commit the cleanup (including removing the leftover rva-sourcebook/ folder that survived the first pass).





renv::init() + renv::snapshot() — user runs, package installs are a long job. Pin R + tidyverse/tidycensus/tigris/sf/mapgl/kableExtra/ggtext/formattable/janitor.
Add .Rprofile (source("renv/activate.R")) once renv exists.
Define a palette + light theme in _common.R — rva_pal (8-hue categorical), rva_seq (sequential blue ramp), rva_ink (chart chrome), theme_rva(). Values from the dataviz skill’s validated reference palette.
Decide the mapgl basemap style — rva_map_style in _common.R, Carto’s free Positron MapLibre style, no token.
r/geo.R written — tigris county/independent-city boundaries for the rr region → data/geo.rds + data-out/geo.csv.
Run Rscript r/geo.R — user runs (tigris pull is a long job). Confirms data/geo.rds writes clean and the validation block passes (17 localities, valid geometry, EPSG:4326). Verified 2026-09-16: data/geo.rds is an sf frame, 17 rows, all rr GEOIDs, EPSG:4326, zero empty geometries.
Confirm CENSUS_API_KEY is visible (Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != "") — TRUE/FALSE check only, never print the value. Not needed by geo.R (tigris doesn’t require a key) but will be for every ACS script from Phase 2 on. Verified TRUE 2026-09-16 via the .Renviron fallback.
[-] Once mapgl is in renv.lock, build one small proof-of-concept map (e.g. rr region colored by aland) to confirm rva_map_style + data/geo.rds actually render before wiring real data into it. Blocked: mapgl is not in renv.lock — needs a user-run renv::install("mapgl") + renv::snapshot().
r/acs_tenure.R’s header comment (lines 18–21) still says “8 rr localities” / “4 primary localities” / region4 — doesn’t match _common.R (rr=17, bhc=3) or the script’s own region3 pooling. Sibling-project debris missed in the 2026-09-15 cleanup; reconcile the comment (and sanity-check no other r/*.R header has the same mismatch).





r/acs_stock.R — ACS B25001 (units), B25002/B25004 (occupancy/vacancy), B25024 (structure type), B25034–36 (year built). Ran clean; validation passes. B25036 dropped from scope — not published in the 2014 window, which would break the three-window trend (recorded in METHODOLOGY.md). B25035 is pulled but carries no pooled rows, since a median can’t be summed.
BPS building permits (census.gov text files) — annual permits by structure type for the rr region. r/bps_permits.R, 2000–2025, cached under data/cache/bps/. Ran clean; the rr17 pooled row reconciles to its 17 members in all 26 years.
Build out inventory.qmd (currently an empty stub). 6 figures, 3 tables, takeaway H2s, bullets, callouts; renders standalone in ~10s.





r/acs_demographics.R written and run 2026-10-28 (population + age/sex B01001, race/ethnicity B03002, household type B11001, income B19001/B19013/B25118; 3 windows, 25 geographies incl. pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17). User confirmed validation passed.
Build out demographics.qmd — 7 figures, 3 tables, takeaway H2s, computed-inline bullets, reliability + race-coding callouts. Rendered standalone 2026-10-28 and figures checked visually. All 7 fig- chunks have fig-alt. (Bullet figures are computed inline; the fig-alt text carries typed rounded numbers that will drift on a data refresh, same as inventory.qmd.)
r/pep_migration.R + migration sections in demographics.qmd (added 2026-10-28 at the user’s request, not in the original plan). PEP components of change (natural, international, domestic migration) for the 17 localities, pooled core/ring/region, and Virginia, 2010–2019 and 2020–2025. Ran clean; validation passes, including a same-vintage match to the Census API for all 17 localities. 4 figures, 1 table, 1 callout, all fig-alt present; rendered and checked.





acs_burden.R reviewed 2026-10-28. Its output was not current — data/acs_burden.rds never existed. Fixed before first run: dropped the sibling-project tract tier and baseline_2022 block, fixed stale acs_income.R refs, switched the collapsed-band MOE to quadrature (was moe_sum(moe, estimate) on an already-summed scalar), added pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17 rows, rewrote the validation block (25 geographies × 3 windows × 2 tenures × 4 categories; rr17 reconciles to its 17 members). User ran it; validation passed.
[~] r/bls_wage.R written (BLS LAUS unemployment + CES average hourly earnings + CPI-U, Richmond MSA vs. regions metros) — not yet run. User: renv::install("blscrapeR") + renv::snapshot(), confirm BLS_KEY is in .Renviron, then Rscript r/bls_wage.R and paste back the validation output. Check that the three comparison metros’ CES wage series came back (a warning names any that didn’t).
Add a bls_cap() caption helper to _common.R when the market page first charts bls_wage.rds (oews_cap/cpi_cap don’t fit — cpi_cap says “via FRED”).
[~] r/acs_market.R written 2026-10-28 — B25003 tenure (not covered by acs_tenure.R, which is race-specific only), B25077 home value, B25064 rent; medians carry nominal + real columns. Not yet run — user: Rscript r/acs_market.R, paste back validation output.
[~] market.qmd drafted 2026-10-28 (7 figures, 4 tables, callouts; replaces the old book’s split ownership.qmd/rental.qmd). Code and layout verified against a scratchpad mock acs_market.rds (real B25118 tenure counts, synthetic medians) — the real render is blocked on the user running Rscript r/acs_market.R and pasting back validation output. After that: render market.qmd for real, re-read every figure, and revisit the three flagged items — the “Home values and rents climbed in every core locality” H2, the “Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest” H2, and the fig-alt text on fig-value/fig-rent/fig-pti/fig-rent-share, all written before the home-value and rent data existed.





One mapgl choropleth per page (e.g. inventory: vacancy rate by locality; demographics: median household income; market: median rent or home value).





data-notes.qmd — public-facing methodology, derived from METHODOLOGY.md.
about.qmd — real content (currently a one-line stub).
Full quarto render completes with no errors.
Every #| label: fig- chunk has a matching #| fig-alt: line. (inventory.qmd is done — 6 of 6.)
GitHub Pages live from docs/ on main.

theme_rva()‘s caption switched to element_textbox_simple() so long source lines wrap instead of clipping. The other pages’ charts haven’t been re-rendered against it yet; check them when Phases 3–4 land.
formattable::comma()/percent() mask the scales versions (_common.R loads formattable last) and take digits, not accuracy. inventory.qmd works around it with local n_fmt()/p_fmt() wrappers — consider promoting those to _common.R before the next page repeats the workaround.





PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar, vulnerable-populations data. The PUMA geography groundwork (puma_core3/puma_region/puma_locality) already exists in _common.R if this ever gets picked up — see METHODOLOGY.md.

title: PLAN.md — RVA Sourcebook build plan
text:
This is a personal/portfolio project, not a client deliverable. It’s a public Quarto website covering basic Richmond-region housing data — inventory, demographics, and market — sourced entirely from public data (Census/ACS, BLS), with ggplot2 static charts and mapgl interactive maps. See CLAUDE.md for session conventions, TODO.md for the punch list, and METHODOLOGY.md for geography/scope details.


Earlier drafts of this repo’s docs (CLAUDE.md, TODO.md, and a prior PLAN.md) were copy-pasted from two unrelated sibling engagements — a Richmond-nonprofit regional report with a much larger scope (PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar pipelines) and a wholly separate Fauquier County study — and never reconciled to this project’s actual geography or scope. _common.R and r/acs_tenure.R / r/acs_burden.R are the real, working foundation; everything else was rebuilt from scratch on 2026-09-15 to match. If you find a stray reference to PHA, BHC-as-client, Fauquier, or a script under r/pums/, r/chas.R, r/mls_* that doesn’t exist in this repo — it’s leftover from that history. Flag it.



In scope (v1): - Inventory — housing stock, occupancy/vacancy, structure type, year built, building permits. - Demographics — population, age/sex, race/ethnicity, household composition, income. - Market — tenure, home values, rents, cost burden.
All from public sources: tidycensus (ACS, decennial, PEP), tigris (boundaries), BLS (OEWS/QCEW where useful), Census BPS permits.
Out of scope for now: PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar, vulnerable-populations data. The PUMA geography groundwork (puma_core3, puma_region, puma_locality in _common.R) already exists from the earlier copy-paste and is harmless to keep, but nothing is built toward it yet.



Defined once in _common.R:







Name
What




rr
17-locality Richmond region


bhc
3-locality core: Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield


secondary
4 expansion localities: Hanover, Goochland, New Kent, Powhatan


ashland
Town of Ashland (place, sumlev 160)


regions
Comparison MSAs: Charlottesville, Richmond, Hampton Roads, DC



bhc is just a variable name inherited from the scripts that first defined it (Richmond’s 3-locality development core) — it doesn’t imply any client relationship for this project.



Quarto website (not book) — _quarto.yml type website, output to docs/ for GitHub Pages, freeze: auto, execute-dir: project. Pages: Home (index.qmd), About (about.qmd), Inventory (inventory.qmd), Demographics (demographics.qmd), Market (market.qmd), Data Notes (data-notes.qmd).



mapgl for interactive choropleths and point maps, backed by a free MapLibre basemap style (Carto or ESRI — no Mapbox token needed). Boundary data comes from r/geo.R → data/geo.rds, joined to whatever ACS/permit table a given map needs. Static ggplot2 remains the default for everything that isn’t inherently spatial.

Repo cleanup (2026-09-15) — remove stale/duplicate files, rewrite CLAUDE.md/TODO.md/PLAN.md, add README.md/METHODOLOGY.md, reconcile _quarto.yml. Done this session.
Foundations — renv init + snapshot (user runs — package installs are a long job), palette/theme in _common.R, r/geo.R, confirm CENSUS_API_KEY visibility.
Inventory page — ACS B25001/B25002/B25024/B25034-36 + BPS permits.
Demographics page — population, age/sex, race/ethnicity, household composition, income (extends acs_tenure.R’s pattern).
Market page — tenure, values, rents, burden (acs_burden.R already covers part of this).
Interactive maps — one mapgl choropleth per page.
Polish & publish — data-notes.qmd, full quarto render, GitHub Pages live.
Future, not now — PUMS gap analysis, CHAS, MLS/CoStar, vulnerable populations.





Every r/*.R script runs clean via Rscript r/<name>.R (user runs) with a passing validation block and produces data/*.rds + data-out/*.csv.

Home values and rents climbed in every core locality

The metro’s 2024 median ($353,500) compares with $383,700 statewide.

Richmond city’s real median rent rose 15.9%, against rose 13.0% in Henrico and rose 11.1% in Chesterfield.

title: Market
section: Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest
text:
Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest









Figure 4






In the Richmond MSA the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the 2024 window, against 3.6 times in the 2014 window.
Among the core three, the ratio is 5.5 in Richmond city, 4.0 in Henrico, and 3.6 in Chesterfield; statewide it is 4.1.









Figure 5






Annual median rent equals 25.5% of Richmond city’s median household income, 20.8% of Henrico’s, and 19.2% of Chesterfield’s.
The ratio compares two medians, not one household’s rent and income: renters are on average lower-income than the all-household median, so a typical renter’s burden is higher than this ratio implies (see the cost-burden section below).







What these ratios do and don’t measure



Median home value is the owner’s own estimate of what their home is worth, for every owner-occupied home, not just recent sales, so the price-to-income ratio understates what it costs to enter the market today. Both ratios divide one median by another; they describe how local prices compare with local incomes, not what any particular household can afford.

title: Market
section: Renter cost burden stayed near half while owner burden fell
text:
Renter cost burden stayed near half while owner burden fell








Figure 6






Across the region, 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more of income on housing in the 2024 window, against 51.4% in the 2014 window — effectively unchanged. 25.7% pay half or more.
Owner burden fell: 20.0% of owners are cost-burdened now, down from 26.1%.
Richmond city has the highest owner burden of the core three (26.2%, down from 33.9%).
Renter burden is nearly identical across the core: 52.0% in Richmond city, 51.6% in Henrico, and 52.2% in Chesterfield — a region-wide condition, not a city one.
The Richmond MSA’s 51.2% renter burden compares with 48.5% statewide and 54.5% in Hampton Roads.

Richmond city’s renter burden moved from 56.0% to 52.0% (-3.9 points), while Henrico’s moved +3.2 points and Chesterfield’s +3.5 points.
The expansion ring’s renter burden is the lowest of the six geographies at 42.6%, but its renter base is small (10,638 households).

Figure 7






The 10 localities with reliable renter-burden estimates all fall between 43.1% and 56.3%.
7 of the 17 localities are omitted because their renter-burden estimates are too imprecise to show; they are mostly small, rural localities with few renter households.







Small-geography reliability



Renter-burden and median estimates for the expansion-ring localities and other small jurisdictions rest on small samples. Figures here use the pooled rows or the three core localities where possible; locality-level cells with a coefficient of variation above 30 are omitted (—) and medium-reliability cells are marked (*).








How cost burden is measured



A household is cost-burdened when it pays 30% or more of its income on housing and severely cost-burdened at 50% or more. For renters, housing cost is gross rent, which includes utilities; for owners it is selected monthly owner costs, which include mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, and utilities. Households with no or negative income are excluded.








What this page shows




Tenure: about two-thirds of households own (67.0%), a share that barely moved, but Richmond city is a majority-renter locality (43.5% own).
Values and rents: the Richmond MSA’s median home value rose 24.1% and median rent rose 11.3% after inflation.
Affordability: the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the metro, and median rent equalled 20.0% of it.
Cost burden: about half of renter households (51.2%) are cost-burdened and that has not eased, while owner burden fell to 20.0%.

title: Inventory
section: Vacancy is low in the suburbs and concentrated in the city and the southern localities
text:
Vacancy is low in the suburbs and concentrated in the city and the southern localities

Chesterfield’s 3.8% is the region’s lowest, and Hanover (4.3%) is close behind; the suburban core runs tight.
Richmond city sits at 8.7%, above the pooled core’s 5.7% but slightly below Virginia’s 8.7%.

title: Inventory
section: The core is a single-family region; density is concentrated in the city
text:
The core is a single-family region; density is concentrated in the city








Figure 3






Single-family detached homes are 63.0% of the pooled core’s stock and 87.8% of the expansion ring’s.
Richmond city is the outlier: 21.6% of its units sit in buildings of 20 or more, against 7.2% in Henrico and 4.6% in Chesterfield.
Small multifamily (2–4 units) is scarce everywhere but the city, where it is 12.0% of stock versus 2.9% in Chesterfield and 0.9% in the expansion ring.
Manufactured housing is a rounding error in the core (0.7%) but 2.5% of the expansion ring and 12.6% of Ashland’s stock.







Small-geography reliability



Ashland is a town of roughly 3,164 housing units, so its ACS estimates carry wide margins of error — 2 of its 11 structure-type and year-built cells fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold. Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities are shown here only where the underlying estimate is reliable; suppressed cells appear as an em dash.

title: Inventory
section: Housing age splits the region in two
text:
Housing age splits the region in two








Figure 4






37.7% of Richmond city’s housing was built before 1950, against 7.4% in Henrico and 2.4% in Chesterfield.
Chesterfield’s stock is the region’s newest: 50.3% was built in 1990 or later, and 17.2% since 2010.
The expansion ring is newer still by that measure — 56.0% built since 1990 — consistent with its faster unit growth.
Only 13.2% of the pooled core’s stock dates from 2010 or later, so the great majority of the region’s housing predates the current market.

title: Inventory
section: Permitting recovered from the 2011 trough, and what gets permitted has changed
text:
Permitting recovered from the 2011 trough, and what gets permitted has changed








Figure 5






Regional permitting peaked at 10,414 units in 2022 and bottomed at 2,520 in 2011 — a 76% collapse.
The 2025 total of 9,091 units is still below the 2022 peak, but roughly 3.6 times the trough.
Multifamily was 3.6% of permitted units in 2000 and 51.6% in 2025; it first exceeded single-family in 2022.
Single-family permitting has been flat at roughly 4,400–5,900 units a year since 2020, so essentially all of the swing in regional volume is multifamily.

Over the last five years the core three localities accounted for 37,448 of the region’s 47,667 permitted units — 79% of regional production.
Richmond city permitted 9,126 multifamily units in five years, more than Henrico (7,549) and Chesterfield (5,857), despite being the smallest of the three by stock.
Chesterfield is the region’s single-family engine, with 8,902 single-family permits — more than double Henrico’s.
The expansion ring permitted 6,719 single-family units against only 371 multifamily, a 5.2% multifamily share.









Figure 6






Richmond city’s multifamily share rose from 50.7% in 2015 to 86.3% in 2025 — the city now permits almost nothing but apartments.
Chesterfield peaked at 57.2% multifamily in 2022 and fell back to 28.2% by 2025, returning to a single-family pattern.
Henrico is the most volatile of the three, swinging between 24.5% (2016) and 73.4% (2023).
The three localities diverged after 2021: before then their multifamily shares moved roughly together, and since then they have not.







What this page establishes



The Richmond region’s existing stock is overwhelmingly single-family and largely predates 1990, with density and prewar housing both concentrated in Richmond city. New production tells a different story — since 2022 the region has permitted more multifamily than single-family units, driven almost entirely by the city and Henrico, while the expansion ring continues to build detached houses almost exclusively. Vacancy is low across the core and the ring, so the stock that exists is being used; the region’s slack sits in its southern localities. The Demographics and Market pages cover who lives in this housing and what it costs.

title: Demographics
section: The region has outgrown Virginia in nearly every year since 2011
text:
The region has outgrown Virginia in nearly every year since 2011








Figure 2






Between 2011 and 2025 the 17-locality region grew faster than Virginia in 13 of 14 years.
The region’s fastest year was 2024, when it grew 1.47% (19,910 people).
Virginia’s growth slowed to 0.24% at its low point; the region never dropped below 0.74%.
Population Estimates Program figures and the ACS windows above measure different periods and use different methods, so their growth rates are not interchangeable.

title: Demographics
section: Migration, not births, now drives the region’s growth
text:
Migration, not births, now drives the region’s growth








Figure 3






Natural increase (births minus deaths) fell from 4,228 people a year in 2010-2019 to 1,451 a year in 2020-2025.
Net migration rose: 7,298 a year in 2010-2019 and 13,035 a year in 2020-2025, so it supplied 63% of growth in the first era and 90% in the second.
International migration peaked in 2024 at 10,787 people, well above any earlier year; domestic migration stayed between 6,069 and 7,543 a year after 2020.
In 10 of the 17 localities, deaths exceeded births over 2020-2025.

title: Demographics
section: Richmond city turned from domestic to international growth
text:
Richmond city turned from domestic to international growth








Figure 4






Richmond city’s international migration rate rose from 2.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 residents a year, while its domestic rate swung from +5.3 to -1.1.
Henrico lost residents to domestic migration in both eras (-0.5 and -3.1) and grew on international migration (7.0 in 2020-2025).
Chesterfield’s growth is mostly domestic movers: 10.0 domestic against 4.2 international per 1,000 in 2020-2025.
The expansion ring’s net rate of 18.8 per 1,000 a year is almost entirely domestic (17.9).









Figure 5






Net migration rates rose in 14 of the 17 localities between 2010-2019 and 2020-2025; the highest in 2020-2025 were New Kent (36.6 per 1,000 a year) and Goochland (35.2).
The region’s rate rose from 5.9 to 9.7 per 1,000, against 2.4 to 4.1 for Virginia.
The 3 localities whose rate was no higher in the 2020s than in the 2010s are Henrico, Prince George, and Richmond city.







How to read the migration estimates



Population Estimates Program migration figures are modeled from administrative records, not counted, and are revised each vintage. Net migration is international plus domestic; domestic migration is the net balance of moves between this locality and the rest of the United States. The 2010-2019 and 2020-2025 series come from different vintages, the second built on the 2020 Census, so the page compares the eras instead of joining them. The 2010 and 2020 components cover only April to June and are omitted, and a small residual (not shown) accounts for the rest of each year’s change.

title: Demographics
section: The region is aging, and the expansion ring is aging fastest
text:
The region is aging, and the expansion ring is aging fastest








Figure 6






The region’s 65-and-over share rose from 12.9% to 16.7%, while its under-18 share fell from 22.7% to 21.3%.
The expansion ring is the oldest geography: 20.0% are 65 or over, up +5.4 points since the 2014 window.
Richmond city is the youngest of the three core localities at 14.1% 65 and over, and has the smallest share of children of the three (17.5%).
Chesterfield has the largest share of children among the core three (23.7%), though that share also fell over the decade.

title: Demographics
section: Diversity grew across the region, but Richmond city moved the other way
text:
Diversity grew across the region, but Richmond city moved the other way








Figure 7






The region’s White non-Hispanic share fell from 58.7% to 54.7%; the Hispanic or Latino share rose from 5.5% to 8.4%.
Richmond city went the other direction: its White non-Hispanic share rose from 39.7% to 41.4%, and its Black share fell from 48.6% to 40.6%.
Chesterfield and Henrico diversified: their White non-Hispanic shares fell to 56.4% and 49.5%, and Henrico’s Asian share reached 9.4%.
The expansion ring remains the least diverse geography, at 80.3% White non-Hispanic.

The “Multiracial” share roughly doubled in the region, but part of that is measurement, not demographic change. The Census Bureau revised how it codes and processes write-in race responses beginning with 2020 data, which raised the count of people classified as two or more races. The 2014 window predates that change and the 2024 window includes it, so treat the multiracial trend as partly methodological.

title: Demographics
section: Household makeup splits the same way: singles in the city, married couples in the ring
text:
Household makeup splits the same way: singles in the city, married couples in the ring








Figure 8






People living alone are 43.1% of Richmond city households, against 30.6% in Henrico, 22.9% in Chesterfield, and 21.1% in the expansion ring.
Married-couple families are 61.4% of expansion-ring households and 54.8% of Chesterfield’s, but only 24.6% of Richmond city’s.
Across the whole region, 29.6% of households are one person — a household type that often fits a smaller unit than the detached single-family homes that dominate the stock (see the Inventory page).

title: Demographics
section: After inflation, incomes rose in every geography, fastest in Richmond city among the core localities
text:
After inflation, incomes rose in every geography, fastest in Richmond city among the core localities








Figure 9

The Richmond MSA ended the period close to Virginia’s median ($86,679 against $93,170) and far below the Washington MSA ($126,684).

title: Demographics
section: Renter households skew far lower-income than owners
text:
Renter households skew far lower-income than owners








Figure 11






Across the region, 45.9% of renter households earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owner households.
In Richmond city, 51.9% of renters and 24.0% of owners fall under that line.
Even in the expansion ring, where incomes are highest, 36.1% of renters earn under $50,000 — the rental market there serves a lower-income group than the ownership market does.







Small-geography reliability



Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities have much smaller samples than the core. 5 of the 30 race-and-ethnicity cells for those five geographies fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold in the 2024 window. Figures here use the pooled expansion-ring row, and tables suppress low-reliability cells (—) and mark medium-reliability ones (*).








What this page shows




Growth: the region grew 10.7%, led by Chesterfield and the expansion ring, and outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years.
Migration: net migration supplied 90% of regional growth in 2020-2025, as natural increase fell.
Age: the 65-and-over share rose in every geography, and the expansion ring is the oldest.
Race and ethnicity: the region diversified, but Richmond city’s White share rose while its Black share fell.
Households: living alone dominates in Richmond city (43.1%); married couples dominate in the ring.
Income: real median income rose everywhere, and renters earn far less than owners — the gap the market page turns into cost burden.

title: CLAUDE.md — RVA SOURCEBOOK
text:
Conventions for all Claude sessions on this project. This is a personal/portfolio Quarto website, not a client deliverable — a public sourcebook of basic Richmond-region housing data (inventory, demographics, market) built from public sources only. TODO.md is the punch list — start every session there. METHODOLOGY.md holds the internal data/geography/scope conventions; data-notes.qmd holds the public-facing methodology. PLAN.md has the target architecture and phased build order.



Read this file, then TODO.md, then the top entry of LOG.md.
Read METHODOLOGY.md and _common.R for the geography/scope rules that bear on the task at hand.
Verify that any prerequisite raw files exist under data/raw/ (there aren’t many — this project runs almost entirely on API pulls). If any are missing, do the work that doesn’t need them and record the blocker in the log entry.





Update TODO.md — check off what landed, add anything new that surfaced.
Append a LOG.md entry: what changed, data surprises, what was left open.
Update README.md or this file if a convention changed — same session, not a follow-up.
Commit the work and the log entry together.







Setting
Value




Repo type
Report / personal site


Commit types
fix, docs, chore, data, content, infra


Scope
A component noun (docs(readme), data(acs-tenure), content(market)). Optional on docs and chore commits.


Versioned
No. Git history plus LOG.md is the release record







Start narrow. Read TODO.md and only the LOG.md/METHODOLOGY.md sections that bear on the task. Do not read whole files when a block will do.
Model guidance. Sonnet is fine for mechanical data pulls, geography swaps, and QA sweeps, as well as page/chart builds — this project doesn’t carry the methodology weight that would call for Opus by default.
User runs long jobs — tigris pulls, renv package installs, and any full render over roughly two minutes. Claude writes the script; user runs it and pastes back errors and validation output. Never babysit a long Rscript run.
Skills carry the boilerplate. Invoke /new-data-script before writing a new r/*.R pull or prep script — it lives in-repo at .claude/new-data-script/. It reads the project-config block from this file, METHODOLOGY.md, and _common.R at invocation.




r/ scripts write data/*.rds and, through export_csv(), data-out/*.csv. Pages call read_rds() only. Pages never call APIs.



Script anatomy: a header comment stating what, source, and output → numbered ## 1. Setup ---- sections → an .Renviron fallback for keys → write_rds() paired with export_csv() → a validation block. Scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. No inline install.packages().

Native pipe |>, tidyverse style, janitor::clean_names() on all imported raw data.
dplyr 1.2 idioms once pinned via renv: .by= over group_by() for one-off grouping; across(); join_by(); reframe() for multi-row summaries. Prefer recode_values()/case_match() for value-to-label recodes over nested case_when(); reserve case_when() for genuine conditional logic.
purrr::map() and imap() over for loops, bound with list_rbind()/list_cbind() (or map_dfr()/map_dfc() if the pinned purrr predates 1.2). Pattern: map(years, \(yr) get_acs(..., year = yr) |> mutate(year = yr)) |> list_rbind().
tidycensus: get_acs(geography, state = "VA", table = "BXXXXX", year, survey = "acs5", cache_table = TRUE). Pull whole tables and build label lookups from load_variables() with separate_wider_delim(label, "!!").





stopifnot() fires only on structural expectations (row counts, all geographies present, no all-NA columns) and on same-vintage published benchmarks — a Census-published table total or another public, dated figure.
Vintage-to-vintage comparisons (e.g. an older ACS window vs. the current one) are a logged percentage change in the session’s log entry, never a stopifnot() gate — different 5-year windows differ by construction, and an implausible swing is a flag for review, not a build failure.
Every data script logs its benchmark results, both passes and variances.





Geography: rr (17-locality Richmond region), bhc (3-locality core: Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield), secondary (4 expansion localities: Hanover, Goochland, New Kent, Powhatan), ashland (place 5103368, sumlev 160), regions (comparison MSAs: Charlottesville, Richmond, Hampton Roads, DC), virginia; and PUMS-ready PUMA sets puma_core3/puma_region/puma_locality (defined but not currently used — see METHODOLOGY.md).
Palette/theme: rva_pal (8-hue categorical, fixed order — never cycle or reorder), rva_seq (7-step blue sequential ramp for choropleths/magnitude), rva_ink (chart chrome: primary/muted/gridline/baseline), theme_rva() (ggplot2 theme; legend.position = "none" by default since 2-3 series use bold ggtext subtitle spans instead of a legend box), and rva_map_style (free Carto MapLibre basemap URL, no token). Values come from the dataviz skill’s validated reference palette — CVD-safe adjacent pairs. Change values in _common.R only, never at the call site.
Caption helpers: acs_cap, pums_cap, chas_cap, dec_cap, pep_cap, bps_cap, oews_cap and others — see the file for the full list. Not every helper has a matching script yet; that’s fine, they’re cheap to keep around.
flag_reliability(df, cv_col = cv) — High at or below 15, Medium at or below 30, Low above 30, from a 0 to 100 CV. Use it for secondary-locality and Ashland ACS estimates, which run noisier than the bhc core.
export_csv(df, name) — writes data-out/<name>.csv. All data in this project is public-source, so no filename-prefix privacy convention is needed (unlike sibling reports that mix in licensed MLS/CoStar data).
fct_wrap(f, width) — applies str_wrap() to a factor’s levels.





Titles are takeaway sentences. The subtitle carries geography, units, and years. Captions come from a _common.R source helper.
For 2 or 3 series, prefer color-coded bold words in the subtitle (ggtext spans) over a legend.
Keep subtitle length to roughly 50 characters to avoid wrapping onto a new row.
Currency uses scales::label_dollar(), and the subtitle notes whether a series is nominal or inflation-adjusted. Percentages use label_percent(accuracy = 1) unless precision matters.
Tables use kbl() |> kable_styling(c("condensed","striped")) with formattable::comma and percent.
Secondary-locality and Ashland ACS estimates always carry reliability treatment through flag_reliability(). Suppress cells with a CV above 30 and footnote the Medium cells.
Every figure gets #| fig-alt: alt text.





Use mapgl for anything inherently spatial (locality choropleths, point maps of permits/listings); keep everything else as static ggplot2.
Basemap: rva_map_style in _common.R — Carto’s free Positron MapLibre style, no Mapbox token, zero-cost. Revisit only if styling needs genuinely outgrow that.
Choropleth fills use rva_seq (the same sequential ramp as ggplot2 magnitude encodings), so a reader sees one consistent “light = low, dark = high” language across static charts and maps.
Boundary data comes from r/geo.R → data/geo.rds (tigris pulls for the rr region). Join whatever table a map needs onto that, in the page — don’t re-pull boundaries per page.
Caption maps the same way as charts, via a _common.R source helper.




Pages ship with takeaway H2s, 2 to 5 bullet findings per section (plain statements traceable to a figure or table), and callout boxes for data caveats. No drafted paragraphs. The bullets should be specific enough that they could be expanded into prose without reopening the data, even though this is a personal project and that expansion may never happen.



Never run R inline. Write r/<name>.R and run Rscript r/<name>.R from the project root. Ad hoc checks go in a temp script in the scratchpad, run through Rscript, never in the repo.
R and Quarto are usually not on PATH. See README.md for the prepend and render commands once it’s written; install paths are machine-specific.
Use forward slashes in R paths, and keep every path relative to the project root.



CENSUS_API_KEY is required for tidycensus. It lives in the user .Renviron at %USERPROFILE%\Documents\.Renviron. Never print or commit its value. A FRED_API_KEY may be added later if CPI/PMMS series get pulled in.
R’s HOME on Windows may be C:\Users\<you> rather than the Documents folder, so that file is not always loaded automatically. Scripts include an .Renviron fallback derived from the current user — readRenviron(file.path(Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE"), "Documents", ".Renviron")) when the key is empty — never a hardcoded username. Verify visibility with a TRUE or FALSE check only.



tidycensus, tigris, and (if added) fredr package downloads are approved. Direct fetches from census.gov file servers (e.g. BPS permit text files) are approved with a manual fallback. Anything else on a government host, especially BLS OEWS/QCEW beyond what a package wraps, gets a quick sanity check before scripting — this is a solo project, so “approval” just means pausing to confirm the source and terms of use look right before pulling.



Not yet published. Intended as a public GitHub Pages site (docs/ on main) once the first three pages (inventory, demographics, market) have real content. No review workflow, no annotation tooling — it’s a personal project.




dplyr::join_by(a == b) on differently-named columns — the joined result keeps only a, silently dropping b. A downstream mutate()/select() expecting b gets a column-not-found error, or an NA after a bind_rows() masks the missing column with a same-named one from another frame. Join on equal-named keys only and enforce cross-name equality with a filter() immediately after, so both columns survive.
PEP — the post-2020 API requires an explicit vintage= argument; year= alone misbehaves silently. Fall back to the FTP tables if the API lags.

(This section previously carried several PUMS/CHAS/MLS-specific gotchas inherited from a sibling project’s CLAUDE.md. They referenced scripts that don’t exist in this repo and were removed on 2026-09-15. If PUMS or CHAS work ever starts here, re-derive gotchas from this project’s own scripts rather than reusing the old list.)

├── _quarto.yml            # website config: freeze auto, execute-dir project, output-dir docs
├── _common.R              # sourced by every page: libs, geography constants, caption helpers, flag_reliability(), export_csv()
├── CLAUDE.md              # this file

├── TODO.md                # the punch list — start here

├── README.md              # purpose, quick start, status
├── index.qmd              # Home

Theming: plain ggplot2 + kableExtra for now; mapgl for interactive maps only. No leaflet, no ggiraph.
Page anatomy: # Title {#sec-slug} → setup chunk (source("_common.R"), read_rds() stubs, inline-scalar block) → takeaway H2s → alternating figure and table blocks with bullets → a closing summary callout.

R and Quarto are usually not on PATH. See README.md for the prepend and render commands once it’s written; install paths are machine-specific.
Use forward slashes in R paths, and keep every path relative to the project root.

title: CLAUDE.md — RVA SOURCEBOOK
text:
CENSUS_API_KEY is required for tidycensus. It lives in the user .Renviron at %USERPROFILE%\Documents\.Renviron. Never print or commit its value. A FRED_API_KEY may be added later if CPI/PMMS series get pulled in.
R’s HOME on Windows may be C:\Users\<you> rather than the Documents folder, so that file is not always loaded automatically. Scripts include an .Renviron fallback derived from the current user — readRenviron(file.path(Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE"), "Documents", ".Renviron")) when the key is empty — never a hardcoded username. Verify visibility with a TRUE or FALSE check only.

title: CLAUDE.md — RVA SOURCEBOOK
text:
dplyr::join_by(a == b) on differently-named columns — the joined result keeps only a, silently dropping b. A downstream mutate()/select() expecting b gets a column-not-found error, or an NA after a bind_rows() masks the missing column with a same-named one from another frame. Join on equal-named keys only and enforce cross-name equality with a filter() immediately after, so both columns survive.
PEP — the post-2020 API requires an explicit vintage= argument; year= alone misbehaves silently. Fall back to the FTP tables if the API lags.

title: About
text:
RVA Sourcebook is a personal project collecting basic housing data for the Richmond, Virginia region — inventory, demographics, and market conditions — from public sources only (Census/ACS, BLS, and other government data). It isn’t a client deliverable; it’s a reference site kept up to date as new data releases come out.
Built with Quarto, R, and mapgl for the interactive maps.

title: Data Notes
text:
All data on this site comes from public sources — the Census Bureau (American Community Survey, decennial census, Population Estimates Program, Building Permits Survey), the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and TIGER/Line boundary files via tigris. No licensed or proprietary data (MLS, CoStar) is used.
Full methodology to be written alongside each page — see METHODOLOGY.md for the internal version of these notes.

title: RVA Sourcebook
text:
A basic reference for Richmond-region housing data — inventory, demographics, and market conditions — pulled from public sources (Census/ACS, BLS) and kept current as new data releases.

Inventory — housing stock, occupancy, structure type, permits
Demographics — population, households, income
Market — tenure, home values, rents, cost burden

See Data Notes for sources and methodology, and About for what this project is.

What changed: Added r/pep_migration.R (user request): PEP births, deaths, natural change, international and domestic migration for the 17 rr localities, pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17, and Virginia. Source is the Census co-est2019-alldata.csv (2010–2019) and co-est2025-alldata.csv (2020–2025) files, cached under data/cache/pep/. Outputs data/pep_migration.rds (annual + era frames) and two CSVs. Design decisions: The files are used instead of tidycensus::get_estimates() because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year (probed: vintage 2025 → year 2025 only), so a series from it would mix revised and unrevised vintages. The two vintages don’t join — the 2019 → 2020 regional step (1,291,900 → 1,316,683) spans the 2020 Census rebase — so annual change is never computed across it and the page compares eras. The 2010 and 2020 components are April–June only (Richmond city births: 765 in 2020 vs. 2,872 in 2021) and are NA. Data surprises:

Natural increase collapsed; migration didn’t. Region: natural change 38,050 over 2011–2019 (4,228/yr) vs. 7,254 over 2021–2025 (1,451/yr); net migration 65,684 (7,298/yr) vs. 65,176 (13,035/yr). Migration share of growth 63% → 90%. 10 of 17 localities had more deaths than births in 2020–2025.
Region outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years (all but 2011). 2024 was the peak at +1.47% (19,910 people), driven by a record 10,787 international migrants.

If it gets confusing, a future session can rename it (e.g. to core), but that’s a mechanical rename across _common.R and the two existing r/ scripts, not a priority.


puma_core3, puma_region, and puma_locality are already set up for a 2020-vintage PUMS pull covering Chesterfield, Henrico, and Richmond city (which tile cleanly into whole PUMAs) plus two mixed outer PUMAs. This groundwork came along with the geography constants when _common.R was first written and is harmless to keep, but no PUMS script exists in this repo yet and none is planned for v1 — see PLAN.md’s “future” phase.











Source
Vintage in use




ACS 5-year
Three non-overlapping 5-year windows ending 2014, 2019, 2024 — the trend convention acs_tenure.R set and acs_stock.R follows. Overlapping 5-year samples are not independent, so the site never plots consecutive windows against each other. Check acs_burden.R’s header for its own vintage


tigris boundaries
2023 cartographic boundary (500k), per r/geo.R


BPS permits
See r/bps_permits.R’s header


PEP county estimates
Two vintages that do not join: Vintage 2019 (2010–2019) and Vintage 2025 (2020–2025), from the Census co-est*-alldata.csv files cached under data/cache/pep/. See r/pep_migration.R’s header






acs_stock.R covers B25001 (total units), B25002 (occupancy), B25004 (vacancy status), B25024 (units in structure), B25034 (year built), and B25035 (median year built). B25036 (year built by tenure) is out of scope for v1 — it is not published in the 2014 window, which would break the three-window trend every other frame in that script carries. B25035 is a median and cannot be summed, so unlike the other frames it carries no pooled bhc3/secondary4 rows.
Pooled rows. Frames that hold counts carry two synthetic geographies alongside the published ones: bhc3 (the 3 core localities) and secondary4 (the 4 expansion localities). Counts add and MOEs combine in quadrature, both computed in the r/ script so pages only filter and plot. Ashland sits inside Hanover and is therefore never pooled — doing so would double-count it.
pep_migration.R (PEP components of change). Never join the two vintages: Vintage 2020+ is built on the 2020 Census base, so the 2019 → 2020 population step spans a methodology break and is not computed — each of the two eras (2010–2019, 2020–2025) is summarized inside one vintage. The 2010 and 2020 components cover only April 1 – June 30 and are set to NA (population is kept). The files, not tidycensus::get_estimates(), are the source because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year. Rates are per 1,000 over the average of start- and end-year population. No Ashland (PEP has no sub-county components) and no comparison metros (CBSA delineations differ across the two vintages). Pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17 and Virginia are plain sums — PEP counts are administrative estimates with no MOE. PEP and ACS growth rates measure different periods with different methods and are never compared directly.
cache_table = TRUE is now a no-op: current tidycensus deprecates it in favor of Census API groups and warns once per call. Harmless, and CLAUDE.md still prescribes it, so scripts keep passing it; drop it project-wide in a dedicated cleanup rather than piecemeal.

Keep this table current as scripts are added — it’s the fastest way for a session to know what year’s data is actually on the site without opening every script.





Public data only. No MLS, no CoStar, no CHAS, no PUMS-based gap analysis for v1. Everything here comes from a package (tidycensus, tigris) or a public government file server.
Three pages, not five. The sibling project this repo’s early docs were copied from split market data into ownership.qmd + rental.qmd; this project combines that into one market.qmd, matching the simpler three-area scope (inventory / demographics / market).
No reliability gate on the bhc core. flag_reliability() is reserved for secondary and ashland estimates, where small populations push CVs up. The 3-locality core is large enough that this isn’t usually needed, but check CVs before assuming that on any new table.




Two prior docs in this repo (an earlier CLAUDE.md/TODO.md pair, and a PLAN.md) described a materially larger project — PUMS gap analysis, CHAS tables, MLS/CoStar pipelines, a 5-chapter book, vulnerable-populations data — that was never actually built here. Those docs were copied from a sibling Richmond-nonprofit engagement and a separate Fauquier County study, respectively, and rewritten on 2026-09-15 to match what actually exists in this repo. If a future session finds a stray reference to pha, puma_core3-driven chapters, r/chas.R, r/mls_*, or Fauquier/Better Housing Coalition anywhere, it’s leftover — flag it rather than trusting it.

The files, not tidycensus::get_estimates(), are the source because the API returns only a vintage’s latest year. Rates are per 1,000 over the average of start- and end-year population. No Ashland (PEP has no sub-county components) and no comparison metros (CBSA delineations differ across the two vintages). Pooled bhc3/secondary4/rr17 and Virginia are plain sums — PEP counts are administrative estimates with no MOE. PEP and ACS growth rates measure different periods with different methods and are never compared directly.
cache_table = TRUE is now a no-op: current tidycensus deprecates it in favor of Census API groups and warns once per call. Harmless, and CLAUDE.md still prescribes it, so scripts keep passing it; drop it project-wide in a dedicated cleanup rather than piecemeal.

Keep this table current as scripts are added — it’s the fastest way for a session to know what year’s data is actually on the site without opening every script.

title: METHODOLOGY.md — internal conventions
text:
Public data only. No MLS, no CoStar, no CHAS, no PUMS-based gap analysis for v1. Everything here comes from a package (tidycensus, tigris) or a public government file server.
Three pages, not five. The sibling project this repo’s early docs were copied from split market data into ownership.qmd + rental.qmd; this project combines that into one market.qmd, matching the simpler three-area scope (inventory / demographics / market).
No reliability gate on the bhc core. flag_reliability() is reserved for secondary and ashland estimates, where small populations push CVs up. The 3-locality core is large enough that this isn’t usually needed, but check CVs before assuming that on any new table.

title: Summary
section: The region is growing, and migration is doing the work
text:
The region is growing, and migration is doing the work

The region grew 10.7% to 1,341,248 people, led by Chesterfield (16.5%) and the four-locality expansion ring (15.5%); Richmond city grew 8.7% and Henrico 6.6%.
Natural increase fell from 4,228 people a year in 2010-2019 to 1,451 in 2020-2025, so net migration now supplies 90% of growth. In 10 of the 17 localities deaths exceeded births over 2020-2025.
International migration peaked at 10,787 in 2024; the latest year, 2025, was 5,387.
Richmond city flipped from domestic to international growth: its international migration rate rose from 2.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 a year while its domestic rate went from +5.3 to -1.1.







Full detail: Demographics

title: Summary
section: The population is older, more diverse, and more often living alone
text:
The population is older, more diverse, and more often living alone

The 65-and-over share rose from 12.9% to 16.7% while the under-18 share fell from 22.7% to 21.3%. The expansion ring is oldest at 20.0%.
The Hispanic or Latino share rose from 5.5% to 8.4%, and the White non-Hispanic share fell from 58.7% to 54.7%. Richmond city moved the other way: its White share rose from 39.7% to 41.4%.
43.1% of Richmond city households are one person, against 61.4% married-couple families in the expansion ring. Region-wide, 29.6% of households are one person.
Real median household income in the Richmond MSA rose 9.6% to $86,679. Renters are far behind: 45.9% of renter households earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owners.







Full detail: Demographics

title: Summary
section: The housing stock is single-family, older in the city, and built out in the suburbs
text:
The housing stock is single-family, older in the city, and built out in the suburbs

The three core localities held 404,918 housing units, up 13.3%; the expansion ring grew 18.4% from a much smaller base.
Single-family detached homes are 63% of the core’s stock and 88% of the ring’s. Only Richmond city is substantially multifamily (22% of units in buildings of 20 or more).
38% of Richmond city’s housing predates 1950, against 2% in Chesterfield.
Vacancy is tight in the suburbs (3.8% in Chesterfield, 5.7% across the core) and highest in the southern localities (Sussex and Petersburg lead).
Permitting bottomed at 2,520 units in 2011, reached a series high of 10,414 in 2022, and was 9,091 in 2025. Multifamily outnumbered single-family permits in 3 of the last 4 years, and was 52% of 2025 units.







Full detail: Inventory

title: Summary
section: Prices rose faster than incomes; renters are no better off
text:
Prices rose faster than incomes; renters are no better off

After inflation, the Richmond MSA’s median home value rose 24.1% and median gross rent 11.3%, against 9.6% for median household income.
The typical home was worth 3.6 times the typical household income in the 2014 window and 4.1 times in 2024. Median rent equalled 20.0% of median income, from 19.7%.
Renter cost burden has not eased: 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more of income on housing (51.4% in 2014), and 25.7% pay half or more. Owner burden fell from 26.1% to 20.0%.
Renter burden is now nearly identical across the core: 52.0% in Richmond city, 51.6% in Henrico, 52.2% in Chesterfield.
Ownership held near two-thirds (67.0%). Richmond city is the only core locality where renters outnumber owners (58,914 renter households to 45,407).







Full detail: Market

title: Summary
section: What to watch
text:
What to watch






Six things to look out for




Growth leans on migration. With natural increase down to 1,451 a year, a slowdown in international or domestic moves would show up directly in population growth. International migration in 2025 was 50% of its 2024 peak.
Home values are outrunning incomes. Real home values rose 24.1% against 9.6% for income, and the value-to-income ratio widened from 3.6 to 4.1. The value measure is every owner’s own estimate, so it understates the cost of buying today.
Half of renters are cost-burdened, and the gap by income is wide. The share did not improve over the decade, and the typical renter household earns far less than the typical owner household.
Production is volatile and its mix keeps changing. Permits swing between single-family and multifamily from year to year, and the expansion ring continues to build almost entirely detached homes (88% of its stock) even though 30% of the region’s households are one person.
Lower-income renters are where the burden concentrates. Renters at 30% of AMI or less number 33,078 households in the PUMS region, and 80.3% of them pay half or more of income on housing.
The outer suburbs are the oldest part of the region. The expansion ring has the highest 65-and-over share (20.0%) and, in aggregate, more deaths than births in 2020-2025 (-1,058), so its growth depends entirely on in-migration.









Reading the numbers




Stock and production are different series. Stock (ACS) counts units standing; production (Building Permits Survey) counts permits issued, which lead completions and can be cancelled.
Small geographies are noisy. The four expansion-ring localities and Ashland carry wide margins of error; the pages suppress cells with a coefficient of variation above 30.
Income-band figures use a different geography. They come from PUMS, which reports only whole PUMAs: Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield plus two mixed outer-ring areas. The southern localities are not covered, so these totals will not match the 17-locality pages.
Migration figures are modeled from administrative records and revised each vintage. The 2010-2019 and 2020-2025 series come from different vintages and are compared, not joined.
Dollar changes are inflation-adjusted with national CPI-U, so they measure change relative to national prices, not a local cost-of-living index.
See Data Notes for sources and definitions.
